title: The Flannan Isles Log
subtitle: Outer Hebrides, 1900
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the interior of a remote Scottish island lighthouse keepers' station in December 1900, whitewashed stone walls, dark scrubbed wood, brass and oil-lamp light against cold grey Atlantic window light, quiet and uncanny, cinematic composition, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no legible writing, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: Flannan Isles, Scotland, nineteen hundred. Everyone knows the lighthouse's last log entries. A great storm. A keeper weeping. Then: God is over all.
beats.img: A thick old leather-bound logbook lying closed and centred on a dark scrubbed wooden desk, a lit brass oil lamp beside it casting warm light, a whitewashed stone wall behind, a small window showing grey sea, the book large and clearly legible as an object in frame, no writing visible.

beats.vo: None of those words are in the official record. A nineteen sixty-five book printed them, credited to a magazine story from nineteen twenty-nine.
beats.img: An old ledger lying open on a wooden desk under cold grey window light, its pages blank and pale, a pen laid neatly across them, an unlit oil lamp beside it, still and silent, no writing visible.

beats.vo: The historian Mike Dash concluded that story was fiction.
beats.img: A glass inkwell and a dip pen resting beside a loose sheet of blank paper on a dark wooden table, a single candle burning low, a rain-streaked window behind showing a black stormy night sea, no writing visible.

beats.vo: The official report says the log ends on the thirteenth. A chalk slate runs to the fifteenth: the lamp cleaned, the oil filled.
beats.img: A small framed school slate with faint illegible chalk smudges leaning against a whitewashed stone wall on a shelf, beside a polished brass lighthouse oil lamp and a full oil can, grey morning light from a small window, orderly and quiet, no legible writing.

beats.vo: The entries were invented. The disappearance was not. The three keepers were never found.
beats.img: A plain lighthouse keepers' room with a bare wooden table and three empty wooden chairs pushed neatly in, nothing on the table, grey Atlantic light through a small deep-set window, the sea faintly visible beyond, still and empty.

facts.claim: Flannan Isles lighthouse (Eilean Mòr, Outer Hebrides, Scotland); three keepers (Ducat, Marshall, McArthur) disappeared December 1900
The widely circulated 'log entries' (12 Dec severe winds never seen in twenty years; McArthur crying; 13 Dec the men praying; 15 Dec 'Storm ended, sea calm. God is over all.')
Those entries are not in the official record (NLB published documents / NRS records); fictional later additions per Mike Dash's Fortean Times investigation; 'no evidence they ever existed'
First confirmed appearance in print: Vincent Gaddis, Invisible Horizons (1965), which credited the log text to an article by 'Ernest Fallon' in True Strange Stories, August 1929

Mike Dash (historian; Fortean Studies 1998, Fortean Times 2017 'True Strange Stories?') concluded 'Fallon' was almost certainly a pseudonym and the True Strange Stories piece was fiction (attributed to John L. Spivak)
The real keepers' log's last entries were for 13 December; particulars to 9 am on 15 December were noted in chalk on a slate for later transfer
Slate notes: the lamp was cleaned, the (oil) fountain full / oil fountains and canteens filled
No trace of the three keepers was ever found; official inquiry (Muirhead, 8 Jan 1901) only inferred a large sea; families 'do not know for sure what happened'; no resolution reported through 2026
